Fever and Rash in a Child

itchy crops of blisters, a rash that begins on the face, or hives partway through an antibioticWhich lesion is it, where did it begin, how did it time with the fever, and what came before it?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Classify the lesion first: among whole-body exanthems, varicella alone makes vesicles, itchy crops at several stages at once; hand-foot-and-mouth blisters are centered on the palms, soles and mouth.
  • Next, find where it began and how it timed with the fever: face first and spreading down is measles (ill, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) or rubella (well, posterior nodes); trunk first as the fever breaks is roseola.
  • When the joints hurt too, date the rash against the exposure: 5 to 14 days into a drug is a serum sickness-like reaction; 2 to 4 weeks after untreated strep throat is acute rheumatic fever. An unvaccinated teenager with face-first spots and aching joints is rubella.

Most childhood exanthems are diagnosed at the bedside from the lesion, where it started, how it spread and the prodrome; serology or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is kept for severe or atypical cases. Scarlet fever, from group A Streptococcus, is the one bacterial rash among the classic six.

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction
Within minutes of an exposure: wheezing, hypotension or angioedema; joints and nodes sparedEpinephrine; an antihistamine alone treats only itch and hives.
Painful dusky skin that blisters, with hemorrhagic oral erosions, days to weeks into a drugStevens-Johnson syndromeStop the drug.
Fever for 5 days or more with 4 of 5 criteria and negative strep testing, usually under age 5Kawasaki Disease covers treatment and the echocardiogram.
Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a face-first rash in an unvaccinated childMeasles (rubeola)Airborne precautions: a respirator (N95) and an isolation room.
3Differential
The classic exanthems
DiagnosisRashTell
Varicella (chickenpox; varicella-zoster virus)Crops of itchy spots that pass from macule to papule to vesicle to crust; starts on the trunk or face, then the limbsLesions of every stage side by side in a well child. At age 3 a child has usually had one of the two doses, so a milder breakthrough case (lower fever, fewer lesions) still counts.
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackievirus)Spots and small blisters on the palms and soles, sometimes the buttocks and limbsFever with painful mouth ulcers; drinks poorly
Measles (rubeola)Spreads from the face to the trunk over several days and turns confluent; palms and soles sparedIll, unvaccinated child with fever of 40 °C or more, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis; Koplik spots (gray-white dots on a red buccal base); joints spared
Rubella (German measles)Fine, separate pink spots that reach the feet from the face within a day; palms and soles clearWell, unvaccinated, low fever; tender nodes behind the ears and at the occiput; in teenage girls and women, finger and wrist pain that may last up to a month
Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease; parvovirus B19)Slapped cheeks that spare the nasolabial folds, followed by a lacy rash over the trunk and limbsWell, after a passing cold-like illness; the rash fades and returns with sun, heat or stress; teenagers and adults get symmetric polyarthritis
Roseola (exanthem subitum, sixth disease; human herpesvirus 6)Maculopapular, starting on the trunk and spreading to the face and limbs; never vesicularWell infant or toddler; high fever for 3 to 4 days, then the rash as it breaks;
Scarlet fever (scarlatina; group A Streptococcus)Rough, sandpaper-like papules, densest in the axillae and groin, with dark lines in skin folds and circumoral pallor; peels as it fadesSchool-age child with sore throat, tonsillar exudate and palatal petechiae; tender anterior neck nodes; strawberry tongue

Joints hurt too: date the rash against the exposure.

Minutesanaphylaxis: wheezing, hypotension, angioedema; joints and nodes spared
5 to 14 days into a drugserum sickness-like reaction: itchy hives, low fever; complement near normal
5 to 14 days after a foreign proteinserum sickness: high fever; low complement
2 to 4 weeks after strep throat that went untreatedacute rheumatic fever
Weeks to months after a painless chancresecondary syphilis
Months after erythema migransLyme arthritis
Rash with joint pain
DiagnosisRashJoints and tell
Serum sickness-like reactionItchy hives that last more than a day; mouth and eyes sparedJoints tender and painful to move but not swollen; low fever; nodes; mild proteinuria possible; starts 5 to 14 days into a drug such as a penicillin, cefaclor or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Commoner in children than serum sickness, and milder.
Serum sicknessHivesHigh fever and low complement 5 to 14 days after a foreign protein: antivenom, antitoxin or a monoclonal antibody
Erythema marginatum: pale pink rings with clear centers that do not itch, usually on the trunk and proximal limbs, not the faceHot, swollen joints, each settling as the next flares; carditis; begins 2 to 4 weeks after a sore throat that went untreated; extremely rare once strep is treated promptly
Disseminated gonococcal infectionA few painless pustules or vesiculopustules on the distal limbs, rarely the faceSexually active; tenosynovitis with migrating joint pain, or a single hot, swollen knee
Erythema migrans months earlierTypically recurring swelling of a few large joints, the knee most of all
Evanescent rashArthritis for 6 weeks or more with a daily (quotidian) fever for 2 weeks or more
Palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, not hivesPlatelets normal; belly pain; blood in the urine
Other mimics
DiagnosisRashTell
Maculopapular rash, mainly after a beta-lactam, classically amoxicillinTeenager with exudative pharyngitis, fatigue, a big spleen and posterior cervical nodes
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndromeTender red skin, then flaccid bullae and large sheets of peeling; mucosa sparedIrritable, febrile infant or child under 5 (rare after that); throat normal
Uniform, painful vesicles and punched-out erosions grouped on atopic skinFever; looks ill
Itchy papules with burrows; in infants, vesicles on the palms and solesAfebrile; others at home itch; finger webs, wrists, around the navel
Maculopapular, with a rash on the palms and solesNodes everywhere, condylomata lata; weeks to months after a painless chancre
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Two blisters on a palm with crops on the scalp and trunk; mouth normalVaricella, not hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseGive supportive care.
A toddler with fever, then a rashRoseola only if the rash came as the fever broke and is not vesicularNo test; reassure.
Mild itch with a face-first maculopapular rash and no vesiclesRubella or measles, not varicella, which needs vesicles in cropsIsolate with airborne precautions if measles is possible; order rubella IgM serology.
Peeling skin after feverScarlet fever peels as it fades; scalded skin syndrome starts with flaccid bullae under age 5Rapid strep antigen test or throat culture.
Rash after amoxicillin in a teenager with exudative pharyngitisInfectious mononucleosis, not a drug allergy aloneExamine for splenomegaly and posterior cervical nodes.
A rash on the palms and soles in a sexually active teenagerSecondary syphilisExamine for condylomata lata; ask about a painless chancre weeks earlier.
Intense itch, no fever, finger webs and wristsScabiesExamine the finger webs and wrists for burrows.
Treatment by cause
CauseAction
Serum sickness-like reactionStop the drug if still taking it; an antihistamine for itch; it resolves on its own. Epinephrine only for anaphylaxis.
Scarlet feverPenicillin or amoxicillin; the rash needs nothing extra.
Varicella, healthy childSupportive care with antihistamines; no acyclovir for otherwise healthy children with typical varicella; home until every lesion has crusted. Acyclovir is for high-risk patients or complicated disease (secondary bacterial skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis): oral for people at risk of moderate to severe disease, intravenous for the immunocompromised and others at risk of severe disease.
Varicella exposureImmune (past chickenpox or 2 doses): observe. Healthy, nonimmune, age 1 or older, not pregnant: varicella vaccine within 5 days. Nonimmune and either immunocompromised or , or a newborn whose mother's varicella began 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG) within 10 days; the live vaccine cannot be given to the immunocompromised or pregnant. In practice: the MSD (Merck Sharp and Dohme) Manual and the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) give the vaccine within 3 days and possibly up to 5; VariZIG also covers hospitalized preterm infants born at 28 weeks or later to a nonimmune mother, and any born before 28 weeks or at 1,000 g or less.
MeaslesAirborne precautions for 4 days after the rash appears (contagious from 4 days before); vitamin A for severe measles or deficiency. In practice: the MSD Manual recommends vitamin A for every child with measles.
RubellaSupportive care; the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine prevents it; keep away from pregnant contacts, mainly in early pregnancy (miscarriage, stillbirth, ).
Erythema infectiosumNo longer contagious once the rash appears, because the rash is immune mediated: back to school; the rash may recur with sun, heat or stress.
Disseminated gonococcal infectionCeftriaxone.
Pause point
Hives and sore wrists on day 9 of penicillin for strep throat Offered as acute rheumatic fever or scarlet fever Are the joints swollen, and did the rash start 5 to 14 days into a drug? → Serum sickness-like reaction: stop the drug
Itchy crops of blisters in a once-vaccinated 3-year-old Offered as hand-foot-and-mouth disease or roseola Vesicles at several stages, beyond the palms, soles and mouth? → Breakthrough varicella after one dose
Unvaccinated teenager with a face-first rash and finger pain Offered as disseminated gonococcal infection or measles Well, with posterior nodes and no pustules or cough? → Rubella
Practice
  1. 4-year-old boy with itchy spots for 2 days papules, blisters and a few crusts on scalp, chest and back two small blisters on one palm; mouth clear Vaccines up to date through 12 months; an older brother had an itchy rash 2 weeks ago T 37.9 °C · playful → Varicella → blisters in crops at several stages on the scalp and trunk after the single 12-month dose, 2 weeks after a sibling's rash, are breakthrough varicella: supportive care. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease centers on the palms, soles and mouth, and roseola is never vesicular
  2. 4-year-old girl whose parents declined vaccines has 3 days of fever cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes then a maculopapular rash from hairline to trunk small gray-white spots on a red buccal base T 40.0 °C · ill appearing → Measles → high fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, a face-first rash and Koplik spots in an unvaccinated, ill child is measles: airborne precautions, and vitamin A for severe measles. Rubella is mild with posterior nodes, and roseola appears as the fever breaks
  3. 6-year-old girl has bright red cheeks that spare the nasolabial folds lacy pink rash on arms and thighs, brighter after a warm bath Runny nose and low-grade fever last week; no sore throat; vaccines up to date Afebrile · well appearing → Erythema infectiosum → slapped cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, then a lacy rash that comes and goes with heat, after a cold-like prodrome has passed, is erythema infectiosum from parvovirus B19; she is no longer contagious. Rubella is a face-first maculopapular rash with posterior nodes, and scarlet fever is sandpaper with a sore throat
  4. 9-year-old boy with itchy wheals and aching joints for 2 days wheals on back and arms; wrists and knees tender, not swollen or warm Strep throat 10 days ago; still taking amoxicillin T 38.3 °C · nodes in neck and axillae · no murmur → Serum sickness-like reaction → hives, low fever, nodes and tender, unswollen joints 5 to 14 days into a drug are a serum sickness-like reaction: stop the amoxicillin. Rheumatic fever brings swollen, migratory joints, and scarlet fever has no hives or joint pain
  5. 7-year-old girl from abroad has no vaccine records Low-grade fever, runny nose for 2 days pink, discrete maculopapules spread from face to limbs within a day tender posterior auricular, suboccipital nodes; eyes, buccal mucosa normal T 37.9 °C · well appearing → Rubella → a mild illness with discrete pink spots spreading from the face within a day and posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes is rubella; the MMR vaccine prevents it. Measles is confluent, with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots, and erythema infectiosum begins with slapped cheeks
  6. 8-year-old healthy boy whose family declined vaccines has never had chickenpox A classmate developed chickenpox 3 days ago No chronic illness or immune problem His parents ask how to protect him now Afebrile · no rash → Varicella vaccine now → a healthy, nonimmune child aged 1 or older gets varicella vaccine within 5 days of exposure, which can prevent or soften the illness. Immune globulin is for people at high risk who cannot receive the vaccine, and observation alone is for a child who is already immune
  7. 12-year-old boy, 1 day of fever and sore throat fine sandpaper rash on neck and trunk, darker in elbow creases strawberry tongue; pale skin around the mouth Tender anterior neck nodes; no conjunctivitis T 38.9 °C · HR 104/min → Scarlet fever → a fine sandpaper rash with flexural lines, circumoral pallor, a strawberry tongue and tender anterior nodes with a sore throat is scarlet fever, the one bacterial exanthem among the classic six: confirm with a rapid strep antigen test or throat culture, then penicillin or amoxicillin. Scalded skin syndrome begins with tender erythema and flaccid bullae in an infant or child under 5, and classic Kawasaki disease needs 5 or more days of fever plus 4 of 5 criteria; he has had 1 day and no conjunctivitis
  8. 17-year-old girl, new arrival without vaccine records, rash for 1 day pink macules spread from the face to the legs within a day both hands and wrists ache; tender nodes behind the ears Sexually active; no cough, red eyes or sore throat T 37.9 °C · well appearing · no pustules → Rubella virus → a fine rash spreading from the face within a day, posterior auricular nodes and hand and wrist pain in an unvaccinated, well teenager is rubella. Gonococcal pustules rarely reach the face and come with tenosynovitis; measles makes the patient ill, with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis
  9. 7-year-old boy had bright red cheeks 3 days ago now a lacy pink rash on his arms and legs No chronic illness; playful His mother asks when he can return to school Afebrile → Return to school now → children with parvovirus B19 are no longer contagious once the rash appears, because the rash is immune mediated, so he can return now. Keeping him home until the rash fades protects no one, and the diagnosis is clinical, so no antibody test is needed first
  10. 14-year-old boy, 10 days after antivenom for a rattlesnake bite urticarial rash for 2 days knee and wrist pain, worse with movement Feels unwell; no wheeze or lip swelling T 39.5 °C · urine protein 2+ · serum complement low → Serum sickness → high fever, hives, joint pain and low complement 5 to 14 days after a foreign protein is serum sickness: immune complexes against the antivenom
  11. 3-year-old boy, 6 days of fever; vaccines up to date red eyes without discharge; cracked red lips; strawberry tongue swollen red hands, feet; polymorphous truncal rash One 2-cm anterior neck node; tonsils without exudate; rapid strep negative T 39.8 °C → Kawasaki disease → 5 or more days of fever with 4 of 5 features (nonexudative conjunctivitis, lip and oral changes, rash, extremity changes, a cervical node over 1.5 cm) and negative strep testing is Kawasaki disease: intravenous immunoglobulin and high-dose aspirin, then echocardiography. Scarlet fever has an exudative throat, and measles brings cough, coryza and Koplik spots
  12. 6-year-old girl with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is on chemotherapy Her brother developed chickenpox 7 days ago Her antibody test for chickenpox is negative Her parents ask what she needs now Afebrile · no rash → Varicella-zoster immune globulin now → an immunocompromised child without immunity cannot receive the live vaccine; she gets varicella-zoster immune globulin as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Observation leaves her at risk of severe varicella
  13. 11-year-old boy with 5 days of fever hot, swollen right knee, then left elbow as the knee settles sore throat 3 weeks ago, not treated Faint, non-itchy pink rings with clear centers on trunk T 38.6 °C · ASO titer elevated → Acute rheumatic fever → migratory polyarthritis and erythema marginatum 2 to 4 weeks after untreated pharyngitis, with strep evidence, is acute rheumatic fever; Lyme arthritis swells a few large joints, the knee most of all, months after erythema migrans
  14. 3-year-old girl has 2 days of low-grade fever and itchy blisters in crops on the trunk, face and scalp, some crusted No chronic illness; playful and drinking well T 38.0 °C → Supportive care with an oral antihistamine → a healthy child with uncomplicated varicella gets supportive care with an antihistamine. Oral acyclovir is not recommended for otherwise healthy children with typical varicella; it is for high-risk patients or complicated disease. Immune globulin is postexposure prophylaxis, not treatment
  15. 15-year-old girl, never vaccinated, with a fine pink rash began on the face; reached the legs within a day palms and soles spared; sore finger joints Suboccipital nodes; oropharynx clear T 38.0 °C · no conjunctivitis or cough → Rubella IgM serology → a face-to-feet rash within a day with suboccipital nodes and finger arthralgia in an unvaccinated teen is rubella: confirm with rubella IgM
  16. 7-year-old girl on day 8 of amoxicillin for otitis media 1 day of itchy wheals on trunk, limbs ankle and wrist pain, worse with movement; joints not swollen No wheeze; lips and tongue normal T 38.1 °C · blood pressure normal → Stop amoxicillin and give an oral antihistamine → a serum sickness-like reaction: stop the amoxicillin and give an oral antihistamine; epinephrine only for airway, breathing or blood-pressure compromise
  17. 4-year-old boy has had chickenpox for 4 days Most lesions have crusted, but two new blisters appeared on his trunk this morning His parents ask when he can return to day care Afebrile · eating well → Keep him home until every lesion has crusted → varicella is contagious from 1 to 2 days before the rash until every lesion has crusted, so new blisters keep him home. The fever settling does not end contagion, and covering the blisters does not make return safe
  18. 17-year-old girl, 3 days of fever pain over the backs of both wrists and hands with finger extension painful, swollen right knee Five small pustules on forearms and ankles T 38.4 °C · sexually active, no condoms · vaccinations up to date → Disseminated gonococcal infection → tenosynovitis, a few pustules and a swollen knee in a sexually active teen is disseminated gonococcal infection: aspirate the knee, NAAT of genital, pharyngeal and rectal sites, blood cultures, then ceftriaxone
  19. 5-year-old boy who finished amoxicillin for otitis media 6 days ago raised, nonblanching purple spots on buttocks and legs painful, swollen ankles Colicky abdominal pain T 37.9 °C · platelet count normal → IgA vasculitis → palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with normal platelets, joint pain and colicky abdominal pain is IgA vasculitis, not a drug reaction: check a urinalysis
How NBME framed it: question 1

10-year-old girl, new to the United States from Central America with her family Vaccine history not given Five days of fatigue, mild itching all over, a low-grade fever and a slightly runny nose Rash for 1 day: began on the face, now covers the whole body No diarrhea or abdominal discomfort T 37.8 °C discrete maculopapules on face, trunk, back and limbs no lesions in the eyes or mouth

Which vaccine is most likely to have prevented her illness?

Competing answers
  • Varicella: itching and a whole-body rash suggest chickenpox; but her lesions are discrete maculopapules with no vesicles, and varicella needs vesicles in crops.
  • Typhoid: fever and a rash in a child from Central America suggest typhoid rose spots; but she has no abdominal pain or diarrhea, and her rash began on the face and covers the whole body.
  • Influenza virus: fever, fatigue and a runny nose fit influenza; but influenza does not typically cause a rash.
  • Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis: a routine childhood vaccine a recent immigrant may have missed; but diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis do not cause a spreading maculopapular rash.
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b: another routine vaccine she may have missed; but this organism causes epiglottitis, meningitis and pneumonia, not a face-first rash.
  • Hepatitis B: a routine infant vaccine she may have missed; but acute hepatitis B brings right upper quadrant pain and nausea, and she has no abdominal symptoms.
  • Inactivated poliovirus: a routine vaccine she may have missed abroad; but polio causes flaccid paralysis, not a rash.
  • Pneumococcal: a routine childhood vaccine she may have missed; but pneumococcus causes otitis media, pneumonia and meningitis, not a viral exanthem.

Down to two: measles-mumps-rubella or varicella. Measles-mumps-rubella: a face-first maculopapular rash that spreads down is measles or rubella, and the MMR vaccine prevents both, so the lead-in skips the diagnosis. The low fever, discrete spots and clear eyes and mouth fit rubella better than measles; the NBME explanation teaches measles, but the stem sets the facts. The options were the routine childhood vaccines plus one travel vaccine, typhoid.

Transferable rule

Classify the lesion first (vesicles in crops, maculopapular, lacy, sandpaper, hives), then where it began and whether it came with or after the fever; when joints hurt too, put it on a clock against the exposure. For a varicella exposure, check immunity, then risk group, then the days since exposure (up to 5 for vaccine, 10 for VariZIG).
